title: Hosea 2:1–13
context: The LORD tells them to say to their brothers, “My people!” and to their sisters, “My loved one!” reversing the judgment names of chapter 1. They are then told to contend with their mother, for she is not his wife and he is not her husband, and to bid her put away her unfaithfulness. The charge is that the mother has gone after lovers who seemed to give her bread, water, wool, flax, oil, and drink, and has not known that the LORD was the giver of the grain, the new wine, the oil, the silver, and the gold, which were used for Baal. The LORD will bar her path, take back the gifts, end her celebrations, and visit on her the days of the Baals, because she forgot him. In Hebrew Bibles, English Hosea 2:1–23 is Hosea 2:3–25. The numbers in this passage follow the WEB.

verses.text: “Say to your brothers, ‘My people!’ and to your sisters, ‘My loved one!’
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “Say to your brothers, ‘My people!’ and to your sisters, ‘My loved one!’” The names are turned: what was Lo-Ammi and Lo-Ruhamah is now spoken as “My people” and “My loved one!” The children are told to say this to one another, a family word that already belongs to the promise of 1:10–11.

Arminian readers hear a real invitation to speak the new names, a mercy already on the lips of brothers and sisters, the judgment names not left as the last thing said in the house.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the command to say “My people” and “My loved one” as the LORD’s own reversing word, the new names appointed by him for the same family.

Shared ground: the judgment names are answered by “My people” and “My loved one!” The verse is a spoken reversal, and it opens the chapter.

verses.text: Contend with your mother! Contend, for she is not my wife, neither am I her husband; and let her put away her prostitution from her face, and her adulteries from between her breasts;
verses.arminianNotes:
“Contend with your mother! Contend, for she is not my wife, neither am I her husband; and let her put away her prostitution from her face, and her adulteries from between her breasts;” The children are called to contend with the mother. The LORD says she is not his wife, and he is not her husband, and she is told to put away her unfaithfulness. The figure is the broken marriage of the land to the LORD, told soberly in those lines, and the sentence continues into the warning that follows.

Arminian readers hear a real call to contend, a people asked to face the mother’s way, and a plea that she put the unfaithfulness away, a word that still seeks her turning.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the contention with the mother, the “she is not my wife” and “neither am I her husband” and the charge to put away the unfaithfulness, as the LORD’s own case against the land.

Shared ground: the mother is the one addressed by the contention, and the marriage figure names a rupture. The imagery is not turned into a new dispute.

verses.text: lest I strip her naked, and make her bare as in the day that she was born, and make her like a wilderness, and set her like a dry land, and kill her with thirst.
verses.arminianNotes:
The warning is given, “lest I strip her naked, and make her bare as in the day that she was born, and make her like a wilderness, and set her like a dry land, and kill her with thirst.” The land is pictured as laid bare: wilderness, dry land, and thirst. The exposure is named in those words and is not described further.

Arminian readers hear a warning still spoken as lest, a judgment of want and barrenness that may yet be stayed if the unfaithfulness is put away, a word that still calls the mother back.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the stripping, the wilderness, the dry land, and the thirst as the LORD’s announced judgment on the unfaithful land, the other side of the contention already begun.

Shared ground: the picture is of a land laid bare and thirsty. The verse is sober, and the figure is not enlarged.

verses.text: Indeed, on her children I will have no mercy, for they are children of unfaithfulness.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Indeed, on her children I will have no mercy, for they are children of unfaithfulness.” The withdrawal of mercy, already named in Lo-Ruhamah, is spoken again over the children, and the reason is their unfaithfulness, the mother’s way now marking the house. The line is a judicial word, not a window into private lives.

Arminian readers hear a severe sentence that still explains itself: no mercy, because they are children of unfaithfulness, a charge that treats their way as the ground of the judgment.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same withholding of mercy from the children, and the reason that they are children of unfaithfulness, as the LORD’s own word over that generation.

Shared ground: mercy is withheld, and the stated reason is unfaithfulness. The traditions can share the sentence without a new contrast from the family figure.

verses.text: For their mother has played the prostitute. She who conceived them has done shamefully; for she said, ‘I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my water, my wool and my flax, my oil and my drink.’
verses.arminianNotes:
“For their mother has played the prostitute. She who conceived them has done shamefully; for she said, ‘I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my water, my wool and my flax, my oil and my drink.’” The mother’s shame is her going after lovers she credits with bread, water, wool, flax, oil, and drink. The gifts are the land’s ordinary goods, and she has attached them to the wrong givers. The unfaithfulness is told in that seeking, without further color.

Arminian readers hear a people who have misnamed the source of their life, a real turning after other lovers, and a word that still quotes her own saying as the charge she can recognize.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the mother’s going after lovers, and her claim that they give her bread and water and the rest, as the LORD’s own statement of the land’s unfaithfulness.

Shared ground: she has gone after lovers for the goods of life. The list of gifts will be answered when the LORD names himself as the true giver.

verses.text: Therefore behold, I will hedge up your way with thorns, and I will build a wall against her, that she can’t find her way.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will bar her path with thorns and build a wall against her, so that she can’t find her way. The way to the lovers is shut. The hardness of the path is a severe kindness, aimed at stopping the pursuit.

Arminian readers hear a real blocking of the path, a mercy hidden in thorns and a wall, the LORD still dealing with her so that the old way cannot be found, and a chance that she will turn when the way is shut.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the thorns, the wall, and the lost way as the LORD’s own appointed stop, his act to cut off the pursuit of the lovers.

Shared ground: her way is barred, and she will not find the path she seeks. The next verse will tell what she does when she cannot overtake them.

verses.text: She will follow after her lovers, but she won’t overtake them; and she will seek them, but won’t find them. Then she will say, ‘I will go and return to my first husband, for then it was better with me than now.’
verses.arminianNotes:
“She will follow after her lovers, but she won’t overtake them; and she will seek them, but won’t find them. Then she will say, ‘I will go and return to my first husband, for then it was better with me than now.’” The pursuit fails, and she resolves to return to her first husband, because it was better with her then than now. The turning is told in her own words, a memory of a better time and a decision to go back.

Arminian readers hear a real return beginning in her mouth, a comparison that favors the first husband, and a word that treats her saying as a genuine turning the LORD has made room for by shutting the path.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the failed pursuit, the not finding, and her saying that she will return to her first husband, as the fruit of the LORD’s barring of the way, his purpose already at work.

Shared ground: she cannot reach the lovers, and she speaks of returning to her first husband. The first husband, in the figure, is the LORD.

verses.text: For she didn’t know that I gave her the grain, the new wine, and the oil, and multiplied to her silver and gold, which they used for Baal.
verses.arminianNotes:
“For she didn’t know that I gave her the grain, the new wine, and the oil, and multiplied to her silver and gold, which they used for Baal.” The goods she credited to her lovers were the LORD’s gifts, and the silver and gold were used for Baal. The charge is a failure to know the giver, and a use of his gifts in another worship.

Arminian readers hear a people who did not recognize the LORD in the grain and the wine and the oil, a real ignorance that is also a guilt, and a word that still names him as the giver so that they may know it at last.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same unknown giving, the multiplied silver and gold, and their use for Baal, as the LORD’s own indictment: he was the giver, and they did not know him.

Shared ground: the LORD gave the grain, the new wine, the oil, the silver, and the gold, and they were used for Baal. She did not know the giver.

verses.text: Therefore I will take back my grain in its time, and my new wine in its season, and will pluck away my wool and my flax which should have covered her nakedness.
verses.arminianNotes:
Therefore the LORD will take back his grain in its time, and his new wine in its season, and will pluck away the wool and the flax that were meant to cover her. The gifts are withdrawn in their proper season. The uncovering that follows is the loss of what he had provided, told without further description.

Arminian readers hear a taking back that answers her misdirected thanks, a real want where there had been grain and wine, a discipline meant to unmask the lovers who cannot give what the LORD now withholds.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the taking back of grain and new wine in their time, and the plucking away of wool and flax, as the LORD’s own act, the giver reclaiming what was always his.

Shared ground: the goods return to the LORD’s hand. The covering they were meant to supply is gone with them.

verses.text: Now I will uncover her lewdness in the sight of her lovers, and no one will deliver her out of my hand.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now I will uncover her lewdness in the sight of her lovers, and no one will deliver her out of my hand.” The hidden way is brought into the open before the very lovers she sought, and no one will deliver her from the LORD’s hand. The uncovering is named in that one clause and is not described further.

Arminian readers hear a public exposure of what she had done, and a hand from which the lovers cannot save her, a judgment that still leaves her in the LORD’s hand rather than in theirs.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the uncovering in the sight of the lovers, and the word that no one will deliver her out of his hand, as the LORD’s own sure act.

Shared ground: she is not delivered from the LORD’s hand, and the lovers are only onlookers. The line is sober, and it is enough.

verses.text: I will also cause all her celebrations to cease: her feasts, her new moons, her Sabbaths, and all her solemn assemblies.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I will also cause all her celebrations to cease: her feasts, her new moons, her Sabbaths, and all her solemn assemblies.” The calendar of her worship stops: feasts, new moons, Sabbaths, and assemblies. The LORD himself causes them to cease. What had looked like holy days is brought to an end with the other gifts.

Arminian readers hear a silence falling on the feast days, a loss of the gatherings she had kept, a word that still calls her to notice who has the power to still the calendar she thought was her own.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the ceasing of feasts, new moons, Sabbaths, and solemn assemblies as the LORD’s own act, the end of a worship that had not known him as the giver.

Shared ground: the celebrations cease, and the list includes Sabbaths and assemblies as well as feasts. The stop is complete.

verses.text: I will lay waste her vines and her fig trees, about which she has said, ‘These are my wages that my lovers have given me,’ and I will make them a forest, and the animals of the field shall eat them.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I will lay waste her vines and her fig trees, about which she has said, ‘These are my wages that my lovers have given me,’ and I will make them a forest, and the animals of the field shall eat them.” Vines and fig trees, claimed as wages from the lovers, are laid waste and given to the animals. The land’s fruit is taken from her story about the lovers and returned to wildness.

Arminian readers hear the vines and figs she had called wages now wasted, a reversal of the claim she made in verse 5, and a word that still answers her sentence with the LORD’s own.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the wasting of vines and fig trees, the making of a forest, and the animals eating them, as the LORD’s appointed end of the “wages” she had credited to her lovers.

Shared ground: what she called wages from her lovers is laid waste. The land itself will not keep her story going.

verses.text: I will visit on her the days of the Baals, to which she burned incense when she decked herself with her earrings and her jewels, and went after her lovers and forgot me,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I will visit on her the days of the Baals, to which she burned incense when she decked herself with her earrings and her jewels, and went after her lovers and forgot me,” says the LORD. The days of the Baals come back as a visitation: incense, jewelry, and the going after lovers are remembered, and the last word is “forgot me,” The charge closes in the LORD’s own name.

Arminian readers hear a people who forgot the LORD in the very days they decked themselves and burned incense, a real forgetting that is now visited, and a closing “says the LORD” that still addresses the one who forgot.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the visiting of the days of the Baals, the incense, the jewels, the going after lovers, and the forgetting of the LORD, as his own concluding charge in this movement.

Shared ground: she forgot the LORD, and he will visit the days of the Baals. The unit of accusation ends on that word.
